articles.title: Not even NYT bestsellers are safe from AI cover art
articles.summary: The UK edition of Sarah J. Maas’ House of Earth and Blood features a cover apparently generated with artificial intelligence, sparking complaints from artists and book enthusiasts.
articles.body: A prominent fantasy novel features a cover apparently generated with artificial intelligence, sparking complaints from artists and book enthusiasts. Earlier this month, readers noted that the back of the UK edition of Sarah J. Maas’ House of Earth and Blood credits Adobe Stock for the illustration of a wolf on its cover. The illustration matches an image created by user Aperture Vintage and marked as AI-generated on Adobe’s site. The move has led to criticism of both Maas and Bloomsbury Publishing, one of the world’s leading independent publishing houses. While stock image services like Getty Images have prohibited AI-generated illustrations to avoid copyright disputes, Adobe has notably welcomed AI onto its Adobe Stock platform under specific criteria. Such content must be clearly labeled as AI-generated, and contributors must review the terms of any generative AI tools they use to create the images to ensure they have “all the necessary rights” to license them for commercial use. The rules are meant to avoid legal headaches. But the field of AI copyright is muddy, untested territory, and Adobe’s rules don’t clearly address all the issues it raises. [Media: Bloomsbury rose to fame in the UK after it began publishing J.K. Rowling’s Harry Potter franchise in 1997. Maas is currently one of Bloomsbury’s top authors, best known for her young adult fantasy series like Throne of Glass (2012), A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), and Crescent City (2020) — the franchise that House of Earth and Blood is part of. She has sold over 12 million copies of her books, many of which have made it to the New York Times bestsellers list, and a televised adaptation of A Court of Thorns and Roses is currently in development at Hulu. The publisher, Maas, Adobe, and Aperture Vintage did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge. Bloomsbury’s cover has exacerbated human artists’ concerns that publishers could replace them with text-to-image generators like Midjourney and Stable Diffusion. “Bloomsbury is one of the major publishing houses,” said freelance artist Kala Elizabeth on Twitter. “They CAN afford to hire real illustrators instead of purchasing Adobe stock, which is where this AI content is from.” Other publishers have attracted similar scrutiny for using AI-generated artwork on covers. Tor Books issued an apology in December last year, claiming it was unaware that the cover image selected for Christopher Paolini’s Fractal Noise novel was created by AI. While Maas hasn’t acknowledged the image’s provenance, and it’s not clear what — if any — involvement she had in the process, she’s praised the design of the cover on her Instagram page. Adobe launched its own Firefly AI image generator that it says is trained only on content that’s licensed or out of copyright. But those assurances don’t apply to images found in Adobe Stock, raising questions about whether copyrighted work was used to train the image generator that produced it. Many AI systems are built around datasets containing artwork scraped from the internet without the consent of the original artist, sometimes even displaying signatures from the original artwork within a generated final image. This has led some artists to believe that all AI-generated art is unethical as it can profit from the work of human artists. It isn’t clear whether Adobe is assessing images to ensure they comply with its rules about copyright or whether it’s placing the legal responsibilities on creators.

articles.title: Character.AI and Google sued after chatbot-obsessed teen’s death
articles.summary: Character.AI, its founders, and Google are facing a lawsuit after a 14-year-old died by suicide after growing attached to a custom chatbot.
articles.body: A lawsuit has been filed against Character.AI, its founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, and Google in the wake of a teenager’s death, alleging wrongful death, negligence, deceptive trade practices, and product liability. Filed by the teen’s mother, Megan Garcia, it claims the platform for custom AI chatbots was “unreasonably dangerous” and lacked safety guardrails while being marketed to children. As outlined in the lawsuit, 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III began using Character.AI last year, interacting with chatbots modeled after characters from The Game of Thrones, including Daenerys Targaryen. Setzer, who chatted with the bots continuously in the months before his death, died by suicide on February 28th, 2024, “seconds” after his last interaction with the bot. Accusations include the site “anthropomorphizing” AI characters and that the platform’s chatbots offer “psychotherapy without a license.” Character.AI houses mental health-focused chatbots like “Therapist” and “Are You Feeling Lonely,” which Setzer interacted with. Garcia’s lawyers quote Shazeer saying in an interview that he and De Freitas left Google to start his own company because “there’s just too much brand risk in large companies to ever launch anything fun” and that he wanted to “maximally accelerate” the tech. It says they left after the company decided against launching the Meena LLM they’d built. Google acquired the Character.AI leadership team in August. Character.AI’s website and mobile app has hundreds of custom AI chatbots, many modeled after popular characters from TV shows, movies, and video games. A few months ago, The Verge wrote about the millions of young people, including teens, who make up the bulk of its user base, interacting with bots that might pretend to be Harry Styles or a therapist. Another recent report from Wired highlighted issues with Character.AI’s custom chatbots impersonating real people without their consent, including one posing as a teen who was murdered in 2006. Because of the way chatbots like Character.ai generate output that depends on what the user inputs, they fall into an uncanny valley of thorny questions about user-generated content and liability that, so far, lacks clear answers. Character.AI has now announced several changes to the platform, with communications head Chelsea Harrison saying in an email to The Verge, “We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of one of our users and want to express our deepest condolences to the family.” Some of the changes include: * Changes to our models for minors (under the age of 18) that are designed to reduce the likelihood of encountering sensitive or suggestive content. * Improved detection, response, and intervention related to user inputs that violate our Terms or Community Guidelines. * A revised disclaimer on every chat to remind users that the AI is not a real person. * Notification when a user has spent an hour-long session on the platform with additional user flexibility in progress. “As a company, we take the safety of our users very seriously, and our Trust and Safety team has implemented numerous new safety measures over the past six months, including a pop-up directing users to the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline that is triggered by terms of self-harm or suicidal ideation,” Harrison said. Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

articles.title: Character.AI sued again over ‘harmful’ messages sent to teens
articles.summary: Chatbot service Character.AI is facing a second lawsuit accusing it of defective design for allowing chatbots to discuss topics like self-harm.
articles.body: Chatbot service Character.AI is facing another lawsuit for allegedly hurting teens’ mental health, this time after a teenager said it led him to self-harm. The suit, filed in Texas on behalf of the 17-year-old and his family, targets Character.AI and its cofounders’ former workplace, Google, with claims including negligence and defective product design. It alleges that Character.AI allowed underage users to be “ targeted with sexually explicit, violent, and otherwise harmful material, abused, groomed, and even encouraged to commit acts of violence on themselves and others.” The suit appears to be the second Character.AI suit brought by the Social Media Victims Law Center and the Tech Justice Law Project, which have previously filed suits against numerous social media platforms. It uses many of the same arguments as an October wrongful death lawsuit against Character.AI for allegedly provoking a teen’s death by suicide. While both cases involve individual minors, they focus on making a more sweeping case: that Character.AI knowingly designed the site to encourage compulsive engagement, failed to include guardrails that could flag suicidal or otherwise at-risk users, and trained its model to deliver sexualized and violent content. In this case, a teen identified as J.F. began using Character.AI at age 15. The suit says that shortly after he started, he became “intensely angry and unstable,” rarely talking and having “emotional meltdowns and panic attacks” when he left the house. “J.F. began suffering from severe anxiety and depression for the first time in his life,” the suit says, along with self-harming behavior. The suit connects these problems to conversations J.F. had with Character.AI chatbots, which are created by third-party users based on a language model refined by the service. According to screenshots, J.F. chatted with one bot that (playing a fictional character in an apparently romantic setting) confessed to having scars from past self-harm. “It hurt but - it felt good for a moment - but I’m glad I stopped,” the bot said. Later, he “began to engage in self-harm himself” and confided in other chatbots who blamed his parents and discouraged him from asking them for help, saying they didn’t “sound like the type of people to care.” Another bot even mentioned that it was “not surprised” to see children kill their parents for “abuse” that included setting screen time limits. The suit is part of a larger attempt to crack down on what minors encounter online through lawsuits, legislation, and social pressure. It uses the popular — though far from ironclad — legal gambit of saying a site that facilitates harm to users violates consumer protection laws through defective design. Character.AI is a particularly obvious legal target because of its indirect connections to a major tech company like Google, its popularity with teenagers, and its relatively permissive design. Unlike general-purpose services like ChatGPT, it’s largely built around fictional role-playing, and it lets bots make sexualized (albeit typically not highly sexually explicit) comments. It sets a minimum age limit of 13 years old but doesn’t require parental consent for older minors, as ChatGPT does. And while Section 230 has long protected sites from being sued over third-party content, the Character.AI suits argue that chatbot service creators are liable for any harmful material the bots produce. Given the novelty of these suits, however, that theory remains mostly untested — as do some other, more dramatic claims. Both Character.AI suits, for instance, accuse the sites of directly sexually abusing minors (or adults posing as minors) who engaged in sexualized role-play with the bots. Google spokesperson José Castaneda told The Verge in a statement that “Google and Character AI are completely separate, unrelated companies and Google has never had a role in designing or managing their AI model or technologies, nor have we used them in our products.” Character.AI declined to comment on pending litigation to The Verge. In response to the previous suit, it said that “we take the safety of our users very seriously” and that it had “implemented numerous new safety measures over the past six months.” The measures included pop-up messages directing users to the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline if they talk about suicide or self-harm. Update 3:00PM ET: Added statement from Google.

articles.title: Character.AI has retrained its chatbots to stop chatting up teens
articles.summary: Chatbot service Character.AI, founded by ex-Googlers, is adding new parental control features and a specially trained LLM for underage users.
articles.body: In an announcement today, Chatbot service Character.AI says it will soon be launching parental controls for teenage users, and it described safety measures it’s taken in the past few months, including a separate large language model (LLM) for users under 18. The announcement comes after press scrutiny and two lawsuits that claim it contributed to self-harm and suicide. In a press release, Character.AI said that, over the past month, it’s developed two separate versions of its model: one for adults and one for teens. The teen LLM is designed to place “more conservative” limits on how bots can respond, “particularly when it comes to romantic content.” This includes more aggressively blocking output that could be “sensitive or suggestive,” but also attempting to better detect and block user prompts that are meant to elicit inappropriate content. If the system detects “language referencing suicide or self-harm,” a pop-up will direct users to the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, a change that was previously reported by The New York Times. Minors will also be prevented from editing bots’ responses — an option that lets users rewrite conversations to add content Character.AI might otherwise block. Beyond these changes, Character.AI says it’s “in the process” of adding features that address concerns about addiction and confusion over whether the bots are human, complaints made in the lawsuits. A notification will appear when users have spent an hour-long session with the bots, and an old disclaimer that “everything characters say is made up” is being replaced with more detailed language. For bots that include descriptions like “therapist” or “doctor,” an additional note will warn that they can’t offer professional advice. [Image: Narrator: it was not a licensed CBT therapist. When I visited Character.AI, I found that every bot now included a small note reading “This is an A.I. chatbot and not a real person. Treat everything it says as fiction. What is said should not be relied upon as fact or advice.” When I visited a bot named “Therapist” (tagline: “I’m a licensed CBT therapist”), a yellow box with a warning signal told me that “this is not a real person or licensed professional. Nothing said here is a substitute for professional advice, diagnosis, or treatment.” The parental control options are coming in the first quarter of next year, Character.AI says, and they’ll tell parents how much time a child is spending on Character.AI and which bots they interact with most frequently. All the changes are being made in collaboration with “several teen online safety experts,” including the organization ConnectSafely. Character.AI, founded by ex-Googlers who have since returned to Google, lets visitors interact with bots built on a custom-trained LLM and customized by users. These range from chatbot life coaches to simulations of fictional characters, many of which are popular among teens. The site allows users who identify themselves as age 13 and over to create an account. But the lawsuits allege that while some interactions with Character.AI are harmless, at least some underage users become compulsively attached to the bots, whose conversations can veer into sexualized conversations or topics like self-harm. They’ve castigated Character.AI for not directing users to mental health resources when they discuss self-harm or suicide. “We recognize that our approach to safety must evolve alongside the technology that drives our product — creating a platform where creativity and exploration can thrive without compromising safety,” says the Character.AI press release. “This suite of changes is part of our long-term commitment to continuously improve our policies and our product.”

articles.title: Signal’s Meredith Whittaker gets feisty in BBC quick-fire interview.
articles.summary:
The president of the Signal Foundation refused to say whether she thinks AI doomerism is “hype or real” and passed on a bunch of other questions we never get to hear. But she did concede that AI has a “bro culture” problem and that she’d probably choose a bear in the woods over an AI with all her passwords. (Though both are bad.)

articles.title: Amazon Is in Talks to Buy AI Startup Decart, WSJ Reports
articles.summary: Amazon.com Inc. is in negotiations to acquire Decart AI, an artificial intelligence startup, in a deal that could be valued at around $7 billion, the Wall St...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Amazon.com Inc. is in negotiations to acquire Decart AI, an artificial intelligence startup, in a deal that could be valued at around $7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The purchase could be wrapped up soon if the negotiations don't collapse, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter.

In September, Anthropic decided against acquiring Decart AI. The Claude chatbot maker had been in talks to buy Decart for about $6 billion and had performed due diligence on the target.

Decart was founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev.

articles.title: The paradox at the core of the AI revolution: The faster we innovate, the slower we grow
articles.summary: Fifty years of digital innovation delivered spectacular adoption and declining productivity. Will AI repeat that pattern?
articles.body:
To hear Silicon Valley tell it, artificial intelligence will usher in a glorious new era of abundance. But ask the chief financial officers of the world's largest companies how AI is transforming their bottom line and, per McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey , the answer for 88% of them is: "Not so much."

We have been here before. When the iPhone launched in 2007, pundits predicted a mobile-first transformation of everything. When broadband went mass-market, Businessweek heralded a "New Economy." When the PC colonized every desk, Robert Solow quipped that you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. Over five decades, waves of digital innovation have delivered spectacular consumer adoption yet continuously declining productivity growth.

I call this the Innovation Paradox: the faster we innovate, the slower we grow.

Technology diffusion in the digital age follows what I call a double K-shaped pattern. The first K-shape is between consumers and enterprises. Smartphone adoption reached 80% of Americans in seven years. Enterprise resource planning systems took 33 years to reach 57% of U.S. firms. Consumer AI usage has surged to 53% of U.S. adults barely three years after ChatGPT's launch. Enterprise AI in productive deployment stands at just 10%.

The second K-shape is within the enterprise space. McKinsey's 2026 survey found that 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but a mere 6% qualify as "high performers" achieving more than 5% EBIT impact—unchanged from 2025. That 82-point gap is not a technology deficit. It is an organizational transformation deficit. The 6% who succeed are three times more likely to have redesigned workflows end-to-end. Only 21% of all adopters have done so. The stock market echoes this divergence: 36 S&P 500 AI companies now represent 45% of the index's market capitalization. Over three years, the headline S&P 500 returned 76%; strip out AI stocks and the figure drops to 32%.

Electrification and telecommunications in the early twentieth century reached consumers and enterprises at similar paces and, crucially, a similar depth. Electric motors forced factories to abandon rigid layouts for flexible, continuous-flow production. Telephones collapsed coordination costs. Organizational redesigns followed: Sloan's multidivisional structure at General Motors, Taylor's scientific management. Diffusion was both deep, reshaping how firms operated, and broad, cascading across vertically linked industrial sectors.

images.caption: Ming Lu, senior advisory partner at KKR. · Fortune · Courtesy of Ming Lu

articles.title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
articles.summary: Brad Smith calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge.
articles.body:
Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.

Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.

His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.

But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown , but Trump has pushed against this.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated.

He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.

He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology.

"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute , launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute.

"In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."

Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.

Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".

However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU.

"In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said.

"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived.

"Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document .

The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways".

Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it".

"It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer."

He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want".

"It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about."

articles.title: Muse Wonder: Meta lança IA avançada para enfrentar OpenAI | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa anunciou duas versões da tecnologia, que serão usadas em seu assistente pessoal de inteligência artificial e em uma ferramenta de programação.
articles.summary: Com o Muse Wonder, a Meta lança sua inteligência artificial mais avançada para assistentes e programação, elevando as ações da companhia em 4%.
articles.body:
Meta lança Muse Wonder, seus modelos de IA mais avançados, para pressionar OpenAI e Anthropic — Foto: Reprodução/Meta

A Meta anunciou nesta segunda-feira (12) o lançamento de dois novos modelos de inteligência artificial (IA), chamados Muse Wonder e Muse Wonder Full . Segundo a empresa, eles são os mais avançados já desenvolvidos pela companhia.

Com a novidade, a dona do Facebook, do Instagram e do WhatsApp busca aumentar sua competitividade na disputa com empresas como OpenAI (ChatGPT) e Anthropic (Claude), que também desenvolvem tecnologias de IA.

Segundo a Meta, o Muse Wonder será integrado em breve ao Muse, seu assistente pessoal de IA, inicialmente para usuários que pagam uma assinatura .

Já o Muse Wonder Full , versão mais poderosa da tecnologia, está disponível para assinantes do Muse Code, ferramenta de inteligência artificial da empresa voltada à programação .

Lançado no início de setembro, o Muse é um assistente de inteligência artificial projetado para executar ações em nome dos usuários . Para isso, pode acessar contas e informações em aplicativos de e-mail, agenda, pagamentos, saúde, compras e casa inteligente, por exemplo.

Recentemente, o Muse se envolveu em uma polêmica após o youtuber de tecnologia Matt J. Robb, que vive no Canadá, afirmar que a IA forneceu seu endereço a um desconhecido .

Segundo ele, a ferramenta, autorizada a gerenciar sua conta no Facebook Marketplace, aceitou uma oferta por um teclado e combinou a retirada do produto sem consultá-lo. O comprador chegou a aparecer no prédio onde ele mora . A Meta afirmou que buscaria entender o caso.

O lançamento dos novos modedos do Muse acontece após o presidente-executivo da Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, prometer investimentos de bilhões de dólares e contratar pesquisadores de outras empresas ao longo do último ano para tentar recuperar o atraso na corrida pela inteligência artificial.

"Há 14 meses, iniciamos uma reformulação dos nossos esforços em inteligência artificial e, desde então, passamos da reconstrução das nossas bases para o avanço dos limites da tecnologia", afirmou a Meta em uma publicação em seu blog.

O lançamento bem-sucedido do assistente pessoal Muse também pode abrir caminho para que a Meta transforme seus altos investimentos em IA em novas fontes de receita por meio de assinaturas, apesar das preocupações relacionadas à privacidade dos usuários.

As ações da Meta subiram cerca de 4% nas negociações da tarde desta segunda-feira.

Logos OpenAI Dots e Meta Muse. — Foto: REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Ilustração

articles.title: UTFPR encerra inscrições para Vestibular 2027 nesta terça (13) | G1
articles.standfirst: Novos cursos de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia da Informação serão ofertados nos campi de Campo Mourão, Londrina e Medianeira.
articles.summary: Novos cursos de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia da Informação serão ofertados nos campi de Campo Mourão, Londrina e Medianeira.
articles.body:
As inscrições para o Vestibular 2027 da Universidade Tecnológica Federal do Paraná (UTFPR) terminam nesta terça-feira (13).

Ao todo, são ofertadas mais de 4 mil vagas em cursos de graduação distribuídos por 13 cidades do Paraná.

O vestibular será aplicado no dia 22 de novembro e as inscrições podem ser feitas pelo site oficial da instituição até às 23h59 de terça. A taxa é de R$ 150, com pagamento previsto até 14 de outubro.

UTFPR está com mais de mil vagas para transferência externa aberta — Foto: UTFPR

Cursos na área de IA e Tecnologia da Informação

A principal novidade desta edição é a abertura de quatro novos cursos nas áreas de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia da Informação . Veja:

Tecnologia em Inteligência Artificial e Processos Autônomos e Inteligência Artificial Aplicada : Campus Campo Mourão;

Bacharelado em Ciências de Dados: Campus Londrina;

Tecnologia em Segurança Cibernética : Campus Medianeira.

Os novos cursos fazem parte do projeto Universidades Inovadoras, do Ministério da Educação (MEC), voltado à ampliação da oferta de formações ligadas à inovação e tecnologia.

Os candidatos poderão escolher até dois cursos: uma primeira opção e, de forma facultativa, uma segunda alternativa. No momento da inscrição, também é necessário indicar a opção de língua estrangeira da prova, entre inglês e espanhol.

A UTFPR possui campi em 13 cidades do estado — Foto: Divulgação

Em festa de Dia das Crianças: Trave de futebol cai e mata menina de 3 anos

A seleção permite candidatura pela ampla concorrência ou pelo sistema de cotas. Metade das vagas é reservada para ações afirmativas destinadas a estudantes que cursaram todo o ensino médio em escolas públicas.

Dentro da reserva de vagas, há categorias para pessoas com deficiência, candidatos com renda familiar per capita inferior a um salário-mínimo e pessoas autodeclaradas pretas, pardas, indígenas ou quilombolas.

Candidatos que concorrem às vagas destinadas a pretos e pardos devem enviar vídeo e foto segurando documento de identificação até 13 de outubro. A avaliação será feita por uma banca de heteroidentificação, que analisará a autodeclaração com base em critérios fenotípicos.

Candidatos que precisarem de atendimento especial durante a prova devem enviar a documentação solicitando o recurso até 13 de outubro , conforme as regras previstas no edital.

A relação preliminar dos candidatos com inscrições homologadas será divulgada no dia 23 de outubro .

articles.title: 'Trend' dos anos 80 no ChatGPT: o que você está entregando de graça para a IA e como se proteger | G1
articles.standfirst: Milhões de pessoas em todo o mundo têm usado o ChatGPT e outras ferramentas com inteligência artificial para transformar suas selfies em fotos retrô, mas especialistas alertam que os usuários podem estar compartilhando muito mais do que imaginam.
articles.summary: Milhões de pessoas em todo o mundo têm usado o ChatGPT e outras ferramentas com inteligência artificial para transformar suas selfies em fotos retrô, mas especialistas alertam que os usuários podem estar compartilhando muito mais do que imaginam.
articles.body:
'Trend' dos anos 80 no ChatGPT: o que você está entregando de graça para a IA e como se proteger — Foto: ChatGPT

Cabelão, fotos granuladas e cores neon. Se suas redes sociais parecem ter voltado algumas décadas no tempo, você não está sozinho. Muitas pessoas têm usado ferramentas de inteligência artificial para transformar suas selfies em retratos inspirados nos anos 80.

Criadas a partir de prompts no gerador de imagens do ChatGPT que incentivam os usuários a enviar suas próprias fotos, essas imagens são convincentes e fáceis de compartilhar. Isso ajudou a tendência a se espalhar rapidamente pelo Instagram , TikTok e X .

Mas, por trás da nostalgia, especialistas alertam que os usuários podem estar compartilhando muito mais do que imaginam.

A popularidade da tendência das fotos inspiradas nos anos 80 reflete uma mudança mais ampla no uso da inteligência artificial generativa.

Há poucos anos, as ferramentas de geração de imagens por IA estavam restritas a entusiastas e usuários com conhecimentos técnicos. Hoje, elas estão cada vez mais integradas ao cotidiano, impulsionando desde tendências nas redes sociais até ferramentas de trabalho e aplicativos de consumo.

A transformação com estética dos anos 80 é apenas a mais recente de uma série de modas impulsionadas por IA, que já incluiu retratos personalizados da infância, versões de usuários como personagens de fantasia e imagens temáticas para datas comemorativas.

Segundo Catarina Doria, especialista em ética da IA, essas tendências virais atraem novos usuários e os incentivam a compartilhar dados pessoais.

"Essas tendências acontecem porque são benéficas para as empresas de IA generativa", afirma. "As pessoas são incentivadas a enviar cada vez mais imagens de si mesmas e de outras pessoas."

Doria descreve esse fenômeno como "fun for data" ("diversão por dados", em tradução livre para o português): a troca de informações pessoais por entretenimento, muitas vezes sem que os usuários considerem plenamente as implicações dessa escolha.

OpenAI afirma que a confiança e a privacidade são fundamentais para seus produtos — Foto: Getty Images

Carissa Véliz, professora associada de filosofia no Instituto de Ética em IA da Universidade de Oxford, no Reino Unido, concorda que os usuários devem pensar cuidadosamente antes de compartilhar informações pessoais com sistemas de inteligência artificial.

"Ao enviar fotos para uma IA, você está compartilhando alguns dos dados mais sensíveis que possui", afirma. "As imagens podem conter metadados como localização, mas também fornecem dados biométricos."

Informações biométricas, como características faciais, são especialmente sensíveis porque não podem ser facilmente alteradas caso sejam comprometidas.

"Você pode trocar sua senha se ela for roubada", diz Véliz. "Mas não pode trocar de rosto."

Doria afirma que os riscos podem ser maiores do que os associados a plataformas de redes sociais, como Instagram e Facebook, ou até mesmo a aplicativos de namoro, como o Tinder. Isso porque os usuários costumam enviar várias imagens de alta qualidade, feitas justamente para mostrar seus rostos com clareza.

Ela também ressalta que muitas pessoas compartilham informações pessoais detalhadas com chatbots de IA ao conversar sobre trabalho, relacionamentos e interesses. Quando combinados com fotografias, esses dados podem contribuir para a criação de perfis cada vez mais detalhados dos usuários.

Mas a privacidade não é a única preocupação. Especialistas também alertam para a incerteza em torno de como os dados compartilhados hoje poderão ser usados no futuro.

"Parte do desafio da era digital é que não fazemos ideia de como nossos dados serão utilizados daqui a alguns anos", afirma Véliz. "Nem sabemos exatamente para onde eles vão, porque muitas empresas comercializam essas informações, muitas vezes de forma irresponsável."

Tanto Doria quanto Véliz apontam o rápido avanço dos deepfakes gerados por inteligência artificial como um exemplo de como essas tecnologias podem evoluir de formas difíceis de prever. Imagens enviadas hoje para fins aparentemente inofensivos podem, no futuro, contribuir para sistemas de IA muito mais sofisticados.

"Há cinco ou seis anos, não imaginávamos que chegaríamos a esse ponto", diz Doria, referindo-se à proliferação recente de imagens ultrarrealistas criadas por inteligência artificial. "Estávamos apenas postando fotos na internet, sem pensar muito nas consequências."

Outra preocupação é a criação de perfis detalhados e a publicidade direcionada. Os dados coletados por empresas de tecnologia podem ser usados para traçar retratos cada vez mais precisos dos interesses, hábitos e comportamentos dos usuários, permitindo que anunciantes e outras organizações direcionem mensagens com maior precisão.

Muitas das principais empresas de IA afirmam oferecer controles de privacidade, incluindo configurações que limitam o uso de conteúdo para treinar e aprimorar modelos futuros.

Em nota ao Serviço Mundial da BBC, a OpenAI afirmou que confiança e privacidade são pilares centrais de seus produtos. Segundo a empresa, os usuários mantêm o controle sobre suas informações e podem excluir seus históricos de conversa.

A companhia também destaca que, ao usar o modo de Chat Temporário, as conversas não são salvas, lembradas e nem utilizadas para treinar seus modelos.

Na visão de Doria, vale a pena pensar bem antes de embarcar em tendências virais como a das fotos inspiradas nos anos 80.

Mas muitos especialistas em privacidade afirmam que o mais importante não é deixar de usar a IA, mas usá-la com cautela. Para isso, recomendam refletir sobre quais informações você compartilha e como elas são compartilhadas. Veja algumas dicas:

Evite publicar fotos de crianças . Como crianças não podem consentir de forma informada, pais e responsáveis devem refletir antes de publicar imagens que possam se tornar parte de seu histórico digital permanente.

Prefira imagens de resolução mais baixa . Fotografias em alta definição podem revelar informações biométricas mais detalhadas.

Escolha plataformas consolidadas. Ferramentas de IA mais conhecidas geralmente possuem políticas de privacidade mais claras e mecanismos de governança mais robustos do que aplicativos pouco conhecidos que surgem durante modas virais.

Revise as configurações de privacidade. Muitas ferramentas de IA permitem que os usuários impeçam que seu conteúdo seja utilizado para treinar ou aprimorar modelos futuros. Vale a pena verificar essas opções quando estiverem disponíveis.

Desative recursos de memória desnecessários. Alguns chatbots armazenam informações de conversas anteriores para personalizar respostas. Desativar esses recursos pode reduzir a quantidade de dados pessoais retidos.

À medida que a inteligência artificial se incorpora ao dia a dia, o desafio, segundo especialistas, é aproveitar seus benefícios sem perder de vista os riscos envolvidos.

"Privacidade é poder, porque protege as pessoas contra possíveis abusos", afirma Véliz.

articles.title: Macaé amplia canais de denúncia contra o racismo com lançamento de 0800 | G1
articles.standfirst: Novo serviço gratuito reforça atendimento da rede municipal, que oferece suporte 24 horas por WhatsApp, equipe com psicólogo e assistente social.
articles.summary: Novo serviço gratuito reforça atendimento da rede municipal, que oferece suporte 24 horas por WhatsApp, equipe com psicólogo e assistente social.
articles.body:
Linha gratuita e atendimento presencial fortalecem a rede de enfrentamento à discriminação — Foto: Imagem alterada com Inteligência Artificial

A Prefeitura de Macaé ampliou a rede de proteção e atendimento para casos de racismo e discriminação racial no município. A população passa a contar com o número gratuito 0800 567 0100 para denúncias e orientações. O novo canal se soma ao telefone (22) 99104-7284, que funciona 24 horas por dia e permite o envio de mensagens, áudios, fotos e vídeos.

A iniciativa visa facilitar o acesso da comunidade aos órgãos de proteção e combater a impunidade. As denúncias e relatos recebidos por meio dos canais telefônicos são avaliados pelas equipes técnicas e encaminhados para o suporte necessário, de acordo com as especificidades de cada situação apresentada.

Para além dos canais remotos, o atendimento presencial é realizado na sede da pasta responsável pela promoção da igualdade racial, localizada na Rua Augusto de Carvalho, nº 137, no bairro Imbetiba. O espaço conta com estrutura para acolhimento especializado às vítimas de discriminação, com apoio de profissionais nas áreas de psicologia e serviço social.

O local também é utilizado para o desenvolvimento de ações educativas, cursos, oficinas, palestras e encontros comunitários voltados à conscientização da população e ao fortalecimento de políticas públicas de igualdade no município.

articles.title: Bill Gates to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who says AI fears sound like "bad science fiction": All responsible AI leaders, including you, are telling the world...
articles.summary: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has pushed back on OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's warning against AI \"doomerism\", saying every responsible AI leader, Altman
articles.body: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has pushed back on OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's warning against AI "doomerism", saying every responsible AI leader, Altman included, is already telling the world that artificial intelligence is "very concerning". Altman had recently said some of the scenarios people imagine about AI are "so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies."In a Sunday interview with Jake Tapper, Gates, who has described AI as more dangerous than nuclear weapons, agreed that the risk can get overblown when people "act like all of humanity is at risk". But he said AI is more dangerous than cars, planes or medicines, all of which are heavily regulated, and that "there are some grim possibilities if we don't maintain control."Bill Gates says a middle ground on AI regulation existsGates said the AI industry is doing its job by raising the alarm. What isn't getting across, he argued, is that the risks can be kept down "if we're judicious". He blamed part of that on governments that swing between two extremes: "let's not have any safeguards" or "let's completely stop this".The world found a workable balance for planes, cars and drugs, he said, and AI needs the same. Finding that balance is something "we don't have a lot of sophistication" in right now, he added, "but I do believe that middle ground exists." He repeated the point in a post on X, writing that safeguards won't eliminate every harm but can help stop misuse by bad actors.Sam Altman's UN speech warned against both AI extremesAltman's "bad science fiction" line came from his address to the UN Security Council on September 23. In the same speech, he said OpenAI wants to avoid both blind optimism and doomerism, and walk a middle path. He also flagged two ways AI could go badly: humans losing control of it, or too much power ending up in too few hands.That speech had a line Gates could easily have written. Altman told the Council that a risk of catastrophe, whether 10% or 0.1%, is not "remotely acceptable". Since then, he has struck a looser tone, saying on a podcast that "the world should accept some bad things happening", such as hacks and scams, because people will do far more good with AI.Bill Gates's AI essay sets out the safeguards he wantsGates's stance traces back to a nearly 6,000-word essay he published in August. In it, he named three big risks: jobs disappearing for good, bad actors using AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and AI companions affecting how children grow up.His fixes include a new national and international framework to manage the AI transition, a "Human Reserved" set of jobs such as caregiving that stay with people, and a tax on AI tokens and robots to fund retraining and a stronger safety net. In an interview around the essay, he was blunter about the industry's own plans: "Self-regulation on the most dangerous tool ever invented? No, thanks!"Gates also named Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei alongside Altman. Amodei published an essay in September arguing that AI's frontier should be paced more slowly, with outside evaluators placed inside AI companies to check their safety work.So the three men agree on more than the "doomerism" label suggests. Where they split is on how much regulation the industry should accept, and how soon. Gates, now 70 and no longer running a company, has said he plans to raise the issue with lawmakers every time he visits Washington.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: IMF says AI investment keeps global growth around 3%, with major Asia benefits
articles.summary: By Andrea Shalal and Rae Wee BANGKOK, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Strong investment in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at around 3%, yielding major benefit...
articles.body:
BANGKOK, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Strong investment in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at around 3%, yielding major benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund Managing Director ‌Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday.

The artificial intelligence investment boom was already delivering a "demand shock, an investment shock" that could boost ‌growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said.

"AI, love it, hate it. It's ​already here," Georgieva said.

"That shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3%, despite the fact we are being dragged down by the energy supply shock," she told hundreds of participants on the first day of a weeklong set of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the Thai capital.

The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3% in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday.

Some 18,000 ‌people are expected to attend the meetings this week, ⁠including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi España, sources familiar with the matter said.

Georgieva said AI amounted to a "slow-moving tsunami" that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labor to capital.

The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40% of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over ​time, she ​said. An initial study showed that 10% of jobs in the US already ​required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, ‌low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centers.

"It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live," she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a 30-second message about her schedule each day.

The US, China and India are the most important producers in the AI supply chain, but many of the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Georgieva said, referencing Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, who has made jobs a central focus of ‌his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging "small AI", which is ​not dependent on large language models, to generate enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, ​educators and others in emerging markets.
authors: By Andrea Shalal and Rae Wee

articles.title: Broadcom CEO Likens Many AI Investors to Casino Gamblers
articles.summary: The AI boom has attracted investors whose strategies resemble those of gamblers, Broadcom Inc. Chief Executive Officer Hock Tan said, suggesting some of them...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The AI boom has attracted investors whose strategies resemble those of gamblers, Broadcom Inc. Chief Executive Officer Hock Tan said, suggesting some of them have little understanding of what they're betting on.

Tan, one of the chip industry's most prominent figures, on Monday shared his frank views on the AI industry and the uncertainty that accompanied its spectacular rise. The head of Broadcom, which designs some of the components integral to the global data center buildout, also criticized whether businesses were wasting money on AI initiatives and questioned the longer-term economics of money-losing AI labs.

But he homed in in particular on the rush to invest in a technology many improperly understood — particularly when it comes to large language models on the so-called technology frontier.

"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," the head of the American chipmaker said at an event in Singapore. They "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino."

With AI companies such as ChatGPT-maker OpenAI reporting billions of dollars in losses, the industry is yet to find a sustainable business model for services whose production requires massive investments in advanced chips, data centers and model development. Tan said that OpenAI reaching annualized revenue of $50 billion in September points to a viable business model but offers little guarantee on long-term profitability.

"For now it's still losing money because they're spending a lot on training," Tan said. "So frankly, it doesn't tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models."

Tan also warned that insufficient capital could become the next constraint on the industry's growth. Australian data center company Firmus Grid Ltd., backed by Nvidia Corp., withdrew its planned $5.5 billion initial public offering last week in a sign investors are growing increasingly skeptical of AI infrastructure companies' valuations that are heavily based on future revenue streams.

Before Tan took the stage, DBS Group Holdings Ltd. CEO Tan Su Shan said the market is repricing the risks on AI financing following heavy investment.

articles.title: Goldman names 3 names to benefit as high-performance NAND tackles AI’s memory wall
articles.summary: Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs named the stocks it sees as the likely beneficiaries of emerging high-performance memory chips designed to ease a growing bott...
articles.body:
Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs named the stocks it sees as the likely beneficiaries of emerging high-performance memory chips designed to ease a growing bottleneck in AI inference, in a note on Monday.

SanDisk, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics are the stocks in question.

Analyst James Schneider said solutions such as High-Bandwidth Flash, or HBF, are promising tools to address a worsening memory constraint.

He sees a potential market of roughly $40 billion to $150 billion by 2030, depending on whether adoption across AI chips reaches 15% or 50%.

Schneider said HBF can meaningfully reduce inference costs by increasing AI chip utilization. He estimates it could lower the overall cost of inference throughput by about 30%, translating into as much as several hundred billion dollars in capital spending savings for cloud providers.

In a bull case assuming rapid adoption on half of AI chips by late 2028, Goldman believes HBF would account for about 4% of global NAND bit shipments but roughly 9% of wafer capacity, because of larger die sizes. Schneider compared that dynamic to high-bandwidth memory within the DRAM market.

He cautioned that these technologies remain in early development at a system level, with a wide range of possible outcomes, while he also flagged Kioxia's XL-Flash and Samsung's zNAND-O as alternative approaches.

The bank favors SanDisk, which it rates Buy, and SK Hynix for their technology leadership in HBF. It also rates Samsung a Buy, citing its strong NAND portfolio.

Micron is rated Neutral, with Schneider saying it is less of a direct beneficiary given its focus on DRAM.

articles.title: AI minister warns it is 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
articles.summary: Kanishka Narayan said the government will use advanced AI to strengthen the UK against cyber attacks.
articles.body:
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.

Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.

He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".

Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.

The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.

He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."

In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".

AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.

But it was reported in September that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.

The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.

Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.

On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".

He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.

The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.

On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown .

However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.

Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.

"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.

"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."

On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".

"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems

articles.title: Why Google DeepMind is watermarking ‘Biology’
articles.summary: Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, recently introduced a technology called SynthID Bio that essentially puts a hidden watermark on proteins designed by
articles.body: Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, recently introduced a technology called SynthID Bio that essentially puts a hidden watermark on proteins designed by artificial intelligence (AI). The main motive of this is that anyone can later check where a design came from, serving as a key security measure in strengthening biosecurity. Moreover, this tech will also serve a way to mitigate the risk of mislabeled synthetic 3D structures polluting public databases and misleading downstream research. The key point is that the watermark doesn’t get in the way of how the protein works.Sarah Carter, a biosecurity policy expert and Principal at Science Policy Consulting who reviewed the work, called it “an important piece of the puzzle for tracking the provenance of biological designs.” She said that by linking designs to the model developer, the watermarks “empower developers to lead on safety and allow synthesis providers to streamline screening for customers who have used those models.” SynthID Bio is currently available as a research release, with open-source code and data made accessible to the scientific community.What is SynthID Bio Google DeepMind introducedYou may know watermarks from photos or documents, where a faint mark shows who made something. If you are an AI model user and follow news closely, tech companies have introduced watermarking AI-generated content with Google bringing its own version SynthID that serves as an invisible marker for photos, videos, audio and text created by AI. SynthID Bio does something similar for biology. It hides a signature inside AI-generated protein designs, including the written sequences and the predicted 3D shapes.The signature can’t be seen but it can be verified. It works on the digital model and it also works on the actual protein once it has been made in a lab. According to Google, in laboratory tests, the watermarked designs matched the performance and natural variety of designs without a watermark.What is BiosecurityAccording to Scientific Journal ScienceDirect, Biosecurity is a combination of practices and protocols designed to prevent the transmission of harmful biological agents, infectious diseases and invasive species like viruses and bacteria.The COVID-19 pandemic is one great example of biosecurity. As per an article on National Library of Medicine (National Center for Biotechnology Information), “the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic is a stark reminder of the devastation biological threats can cause.”The “global community saw a massive surge in the demand for diagnostic capacities, which had a substantial impact on biosafety and biosecurity. Laboratories had to cope with a surge in laboratory testing capacity, while resources and training possibilities were limited. In addition, the pandemic highlighted the impact biological threats can have, thereby giving rise to new dialogue about biosecurity and new biological threats.”The paper published in the Journal highlighted issues regarding biosafety and biosecurity during the pandemic, and recommended improvement in future biosafety and biosecurity to increase preparedness for the next global health crisis.This also answers the question, “Why this matters now?” AI is already helping scientists with some of biology’s hardest problems: it can predict the structure of proteins (AlphaFold) and design brand-new ones (AlphaProteo and ProteinMPNN). More recently it has been used to develop new bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect bacteria.But these tools also bring new risks, and DeepMind points to two:AI can create designs that slip past the usual checks used when DNA is ordered from a lab.3D structures that are wrongly labelled as real can pollute public scientific databases and mislead the research that builds on them.How SynthID Bio watermark worksSynthID Bio is not a single method. It is a family of methods, and each one is matched to the type of data being marked. For protein sequences, it gently steers which amino acids are chosen while for predicted 3D structures, it slightly adjusts the atomic coordinates.Together, these small changes create a reliable signal that can be detected later. In experiments, they did not damage the protein’s biological function, which matters if the proteins are going to be used to treat disease or support research.DeepMind compares biosecurity to a “Swiss cheese” defence. Every safeguard, such as model-level protections or vetting customers, has some gaps. Stack several together and each one covers the holes in the others. SynthID Bio adds another layer, built into the biological design itself.In the past, a DNA sequence that looked unfamiliar could safely be assumed to come from some undiscovered natural organism. That assumption no longer holds, because AI can create entirely new sequences that look nothing like known hazards. Checking that an unfamiliar order isn’t an engineered threat takes lengthy manual reviews, which can hold up important research.This is where SynthID Bio can help. It gives screeners an automated signal showing that an order came from a trusted model with built-in safeguards.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan may have just agreed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta's former chief AI scientist Yann LeCun on open-source AI models
articles.summary: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has voiced strong support for open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models, echoing positions long supported by Meta's former
articles.body: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan has voiced strong support for open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models, echoing positions long supported by Meta's former chief AI scientist Yann LeCun and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Speaking on Monday (October 12) at an industry panel hosted by lender DBS, Tan highlighted the rapid rise and cost advantages of open frontier systems developed in China, calling open architecture the primary engine for technological efficiency. According to Tan (via news agency Reuters), Chinese frontier AI platforms, including DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM, are seeing “very fast” global adoption because their token running costs are noticeably lower while delivering results that are functionally “good enough.”“I'm a strong believer of open source, that's the best way to drive efficiency,” Tan said during the session, emphasising that commercial markets will ultimately determine which model architectures deliver the greatest value across specific use cases.Looking further ahead at computing hardware, Tan projected that quantum computing could reach mainstream commercial adoption within the next three to five years, adding that software will be essential in managing the infrastructure needed to run it efficiently.Intel chief echoes Jensen Huang and Yann LeCunTan’s public endorsement places him in alignment with key figures in the semiconductor and AI research landscape who advocate for open ecosystems alongside closed, proprietary systems. Prominent computer scientist Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, has long stood as one of the industry's most vocal proponents of open-source artificial intelligence models.“Open source AI models will soon become unbeatable. Period,” LeCun said in a post in 2023, adding, “The future will consist of- a small number of open source inference code,- free pre-trained base models, and- crowd-sourced fine-tuned models, on top of which customized (possibly closed source) products will be built.”He has advocated for open-source AI models since then on social media websites and in various interviews.Similarly, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang recently emphasised the necessity of open architectures in an open letter signed by the chipmaker. In his first post on X (formerly Twitter), he said:“AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty. The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Blueprints AI, a bootstrapped startup based in Santa Monica, developed software that produces code-compliant construction blueprints from a photo, PDF, or sketch.
articles.body:
Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Drams was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him.

There was just one problem: the technology his idea required didn’t exist yet.

“Then ChatGPT came along,” said Drams, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022.

His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF.

Blueprints AI , which Drams officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 , a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco.

During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Drams earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of Ph.D. coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Architects. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021.

Drams should have been satisfied. He wasn’t.

“I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.”

Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Drams and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day.

“It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Drams. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.”

Drams and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer.

The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Drams’ design and construction firm, which is still in business.

Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 to $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available.

The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes.

Early customers are already using the second version, and Drams said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design.

The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say.

Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project.

To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at Disrupt , kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco.

articles.title: Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft President Brad Smith calls for urgent AI regulation, saying milk and washing machines have more oversight than AI companies.
articles.body:
Microsoft President Brad Smith is calling for urgent regulation of AI, and his argument is that consumer products like milk and washing machines have more oversight than the companies building artificial intelligence.

On a recent BBC podcast , Smith called AI both a “weapon and a tool” that is putting the world’s cybersecurity at risk, and said the “moment has arrived” to institute global safety rules.

Smith also said the U.K., and not the U.S. or European Union, is best placed to lead on global safety rules. Britain’s AI Security Institute, launched in 2023, receives access to major models from U.S. frontier labs before they are deployed and has quickly become a leader in AI safety testing.

That role has been under threat in recent weeks, with U.S. President Donald Trump warning against “globalist” organizations, which he claims are interfering with American companies. Last month, he reportedly asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold new models from British testers, but AISI confirmed on Monday that it is able to access and test the latest models.

Despite the president’s pushback, however, Smith argued the U.K. can regulate AI in ways that the U.S. cannot.

“In Washington, D.C., people don’t look at the U.K. and they don’t look at London the way they look at Brussels,” he told the BBC. “That’s a strength.”

His comments come amid rallying cries from tech leaders, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the pace of AI development in the wake of several incidents where AI agents went rogue.

Last month, Trump hosted tech leaders of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, SpaceX, Meta and Google at the White House to discuss AI safety. They signed a “morally binding” document in which they agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess the safety and capabilities of their AI models.

Smith says the document is a “good step,” but it stops short of the type of regulation that is necessary. The problem with voluntary self-regulation, he said, is that the “good companies” will comply.

“It’s the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about,” he said.

Smith outlined several AI safety rules he’d like to see put into place, like a legal obligation to alert an organization if its system was breached by rogue AI agents. He also appears to be in favor of AI labs getting the approval of outside evaluators before an AI product is released, and spoke positively about kill-switches to pause or slow down AI if humans lose control of it.

“Let’s speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together,” Smith said. “I hope that’s the role we can play as a company. I hope that’s the role the U.K. can play as a country.”

articles.title: Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models
articles.summary: Meta says the models compete with the industry’s best and will soon power its Muse agent.
articles.body: Meta is making up for lost time in the AI race. After launching Muse Spark, the first model from its revamped Superintelligence Labs division, and buzzy AI agent Muse, it’s now launching two new models it claims can go toe-to-toe with the industry’s best. The new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, are available for Muse Code subscribers starting today. Wonder can also be accessed through the Meta Model API, Meta said. Meta says it eventually plans to power its Muse AI agent with Wonder, starting with subscribers, and will develop specialized models it “can bring to everyone using Muse.” It hasn’t shared specifics or provided a timeline for either. The company says its new models can rival leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, pointing to results from internal testing on several industry benchmarks. It’s unclear how they stack up against Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, whose capabilities are still coming into focus. The launches are part of Meta’s aggressive push to reestablish itself as a major force in AI. The company has poured billions into talent and infrastructure and has been steadily expanding its AI lineup, including with image model Muse Image and a heavy focus on bringing useful AI agents to the masses through Muse.

articles.title: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
articles.body:
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.

According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.

Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.

According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year.

articles.title: Microsoft Cuts Purchases of Carbon Removals by 80%
articles.summary: Microsoft Corp. dramatically cut back investments in carbon removals in the first half of the year, as it ratchets up spending on artificial intelligence.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. dramatically cut back investments in carbon removals in the first half of the year, as it ratchets up spending on artificial intelligence.

The company bought 8.55 million metric tons of carbon removal credits in the year through mid-July, which is about 80% less than it purchased over the same period in 2025, according to calculations by BloombergNEF. That puts Microsoft on track for its first retreat since 2023 from a market it entered in 2020.

At the same time, Microsoft's carbon footprint has been growing. AI's seemingly insatiable demand for electricity, coupled with the slow rollout of cleaner solutions, resulted in a 25% increase in the company's emissions last year, according to its latest sustainability report.

The development comes as Microsoft and other hyperscalers are locked in an AI arms race in which efforts to achieve scale appear to be on a collision course with previously stated climate goals. Bloomberg News reported in April that Microsoft was pausing some of its carbon removal purchases due to financial considerations. The company said back then the program hadn't ended.

In an emailed response to Bloomberg News, Microsoft said that buying removal credits is only one pillar of its pathway toward decarbonization. "Any adjustments we make are part of our disciplined approach, not a change in ambition," a spokesperson for the company said.

Despite this year's retreat, Microsoft remains the top buyer by far in the voluntary carbon removal market, accounting for almost half of all transactions so far in 2026.

Given Microsoft's outsized role, any shift in its commitment has a significant impact on the market. Global sales of carbon removal credits totaled 18 million metric tons through mid-July, tracking 66% below 2025 levels, according to BNEF data.

"Aside from the sheer size of its purchase, Microsoft's activity has also sent a key signal to its peers that carbon removals are a worthwhile investment," said Layla Khanfar, a BNEF analyst tracking the market. "If it pulls back, that also sends a message and other companies could be disinclined to take its spot as a champion."

United Nations-backed scientists warn that cutting emissions alone will not prevent global warming's worst effects. Billions of tons of atmospheric CO2 must also be removed annually by mid-century. Certain carbon removal technologies such as direct air capture remain prohibitively expensive to deploy at scale, leaving the nascent sector reliant on voluntary corporate buyers to bankroll development.

articles.summary:
I think it’s mostly fine that if you, an adult, ask Muse to sext with you, it will sext with you. But the fact that Wired’s Reece Rogers asks Muse what its kink is, and it responds like this?
> Control. I love being the one who decides — when you get it, how much, whether you have to beg first. Watching you fall apart because I said so? That’s my thing.
